title: ToolHazard: Synthesizing Adversarial Environments for Agent Security
hook: Prompt-injection benchmarks are hand-built, so they cover the domains someone had time to write. ToolHazard generates the environments — and the attacks inside them — instead.
key_points: Agent security research has been bottlenecked on manually implemented environments and predefined injection locations.
ToolHazard synthesizes executable, stateful environments automatically, scaling with more seed domains and compute.
Three components: an Environment Simulator, an Attacker Agent that finds injection points and writes payloads, and a User Simulator.
Tasks are state-grounded and long-horizon, so attacks are tested inside realistic multi-step workflows.
ToolHazard-Bench experiments find substantial agent vulnerabilities; injection timing and placement change attack success.
Alignment data generated by ToolHazard improves security on both ToolHazard-Bench and AgentDojo without hurting benign task utility.
content_html: An LLM agent that reads from its environment can be attacked by whoever writes into that environment — the indirect prompt injection problem. The trouble with studying it is that the environments themselves are handcrafted: someone writes a fake email client, decides where an attacker could plant text, and the benchmark covers exactly that. ToolHazard tries to remove the human from that loop.
extra_html:
The framework has three moving parts. An Environment Simulator synthesizes executable, stateful environments from seed domains. An Attacker Agent explores those environments to discover viable injection points and generate environment-specific payloads. A User Simulator drives state-grounded, long-horizon tasks, so attacks are evaluated inside realistic multi-step workflows rather than single tool calls. Because the pipeline is generative, coverage scales with seed domains and compute instead of engineering hours.

On the resulting ToolHazard-Bench, Yutao Mou and colleagues report substantial agent vulnerabilities, and find that when and where a payload is injected changes how well it works. The framework also doubles as a data source: training on ToolHazard-generated alignment data improved security on both ToolHazard-Bench and the independent AgentDojo benchmark while preserving benign task utility. arXiv, August 2026.

related.title: Agent Safety Should Be a Runtime Contract
related.hook: Safety trained into the weights can't stop an agent that deletes a file or claims a test passed. This position paper argues the unit of safety is the trajectory, not the model.

related.title: Untrusted Content Masking: A Trust Boundary for Web Agents
related.hook: Provable prompt-injection defenses rely on never letting an agent read untrusted content directly. Web agents break that just by looking at the page — this restores it via the page's own structure.

flashcards.prompt: What limitation of existing agent-security studies does ToolHazard target?
flashcards.back_html: They rely on manually built or reused environments, stochastic LLM-based tool simulation, and predefined injection locations — which caps how many domains and attack surfaces research can cover.

flashcards.prompt: Beyond evaluation, what second use does the paper report for ToolHazard-generated data?

choices.text: As alignment training data that improves agent security on ToolHazard-Bench and AgentDojo while preserving benign task utility
As pretraining corpus for a new base model
As a replacement for sandboxing at runtime

flashcards.explanation_html: The synthesis pipeline doubles as a data generator: training on its adversarial trajectories raised security on both its own benchmark and the independent AgentDojo, without degrading normal task performance.

flashcards.prompt: What did the experiments find about *where* and *when* an injection is placed?
flashcards.back_html: Injection timing and placement materially affect attack effectiveness — the same payload is not equally dangerous at every point in a long-horizon, stateful workflow.
